question: What did prospects say about data residency?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every statement the prospect makes or asks about data residency, including where data is stored or hosted, regional or EU hosting requirements, data sovereignty or GDPR concerns, and any requirements, objections, or concerns they raise. Also extract every answer or claim OrbitFlow staff give about data residency, including hedges, options offered, and any commitments or corrections. If the topic is not discussed, say so.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as the Prospect call type (new business).
Data residency synonyms include data location, sovereignty, regional hosting, and GDPR-related storage concerns.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We don't have a special data-residency requirement for this project.
findings.context: Prospect (Tom Alvarez, Acme Logistics) stated Acme has no special data-residency requirement for this project. — Customer's own statement; the only direct residency statement by a prospect in this call. Says it applies to this project, not necessarily company-wide.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU residency available on Enterprise if you ever need it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow (Jon Bell) said EU data residency is available on the Enterprise tier if the customer ever needs it. — Vendor offer in response to Tom's security questions. Framed as an optional Enterprise feature, not a default. No details on regions, storage, or processing location beyond EU.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We're not healthcare.
findings.context: Tom said Acme is not in healthcare, which is why its security/compliance list is short. This implies no sector-driven residency rules, but the call does not state that directly. — Related to residency only by implication; the prospect did not mention residency in this turn.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: what happens to data sent to an LLM provider is a question you'll get from your security team, and the honest answer is it depends on configuration and provider
findings.context: OrbitFlow (Jon Bell) hedged on where data goes when sent to an LLM provider: the answer depends on configuration and provider; they use enterprise API arrangements where available and document subprocessors. He offered to disable AI or scope the pilot to deterministic steps if policy is strict. — Not a residency commitment; about third-party LLM data handling. Location of processing is left open and was not stated as a commitment.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: EU. We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
findings.context: Prospect (Elliot Greene) raised EU/UK data residency: BrightPath is a US operation with a UK subsidiary, and he asked what the default data region is. — Prospect's direct residency question during the security section, raised in response to the vendor's EU residency claim.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU data residency available on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow (Jon Bell) said EU data residency is available on the Enterprise tier. — Vendor's baseline security capability list, given in answer to the security requirements on the call; a product claim, not a contractual commitment.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: Default depends on where the workspace is provisioned. I'd rather confirm the specifics in writing than guess at your architecture on a call.
findings.context: OrbitFlow (Jon Bell) would not state the default data region; he said it depends on where the workspace is provisioned and committed to confirming the specifics in writing rather than on the call. — Hedge on the residency question. Vendor declined to guess at the prospect's architecture; written answer is an open item.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: Good. That's the right answer.
findings.context: Prospect approved of the vendor declining to give a residency default verbally, favouring a written answer. — Reaction to the vendor's hedge; signals the prospect will require a written residency position, not a verbal one.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: confirm how US data is handled
findings.context: Prospect's security list included confirming how US data is handled, separate from EU residency. — Listed as one of five security items in the opening agenda; the call does not return to US-specific handling in detail.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: And because we sell into the UK and EU I want to understand where customer data actually gets processed.
findings.context: Prospect (Sophie Reed) states Cedar & Finch sells into the UK and EU, and wants to understand where customer data is processed. — Customer's own data residency concern; raised during security questions.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: UK and EU, yes. Which is a security question, so let me do that bit now while I remember.
findings.context: Prospect confirms the business operates in UK and EU. — Answer to vendor question about geography; sets up residency concern.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff states EU data residency is available only on the Enterprise plan; for Growth plan he would need to confirm the default processing region in writing rather than guess. — Partial answer; Growth default region unconfirmed.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Enterprise. That's the expensive one.
findings.context: Prospect reacts that EU residency requires Enterprise, which is the expensive tier. — Price implication of residency requirement.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: That's the expensive one, yes.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff confirms Enterprise is the expensive one, acknowledging the residency tier cost. — Vendor acknowledgement of tier cost.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I'll also get you written answers on the Shopify trigger coverage and the default processing region. Those are the two I dodged.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff commits to giving written answer on default processing region, deferring it as one of two dodged questions. — Open follow-up commitment on data location.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: German or EU data residency
findings.context: Prospect's IT governance lead listed German or EU data residency as a headline governance requirement. — Customer requirement raised during governance discussion; stated as a list item, not yet a hard decision.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states EU data residency is available on the Enterprise package. — Vendor answer to the governance checklist; scoped to EU, not Germany.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I said German or EU. Which is it?
findings.context: Prospect pressed the vendor to clarify whether it meant German or EU residency. — Customer asked for a precise answer after the vendor's EU claim.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU. I am not going to tell you we have a German region because we don't.
findings.context: OrbitFlow clarified it offers EU residency only and does not have a German region. — Vendor correction/clarification that narrows the earlier claim; explicitly declines to claim German hosting.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: EU may be sufficient. It depends on which entity the data belongs to, and that is a question for our legal team, not for you.
findings.context: Prospect says EU residency may be sufficient but depends on which legal entity owns the data, which needs legal review. — Customer's conditional acceptance; final sufficiency depends on their legal team, not the vendor.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: two German plants are still prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors
findings.context: Prospect states two German plants are prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors, so cloud-first is policy rather than reality. — Related hosting/exposure constraint rather than a pure residency requirement; the customer later says this was from memory and not verified against current policy (T257).

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: EU residency for European records
findings.context: Ember's Hannah Cole requires EU residency for European records as part of the auditability gate. — Listed among the audit and security requirements Hannah needs satisfied; the call does not state Ember's location or which records are European.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency available on Enterprise.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's Nina Patel states EU data residency is available on the Enterprise plan. — Answer to Hannah's security checklist; given as a plan-tier feature, not a general capability. No details on hosting location or granularity were given.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Security pack — SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation, encryption details.
findings.context: Data residency is not among the items Leo Grant committed to send, so the EU residency answer has no written follow-up in the call. — Leo's list of owed items names the security pack contents but does not include residency. This is an inference from the omission.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: normal GDPR terms, and — this one matters — written reassurance that our client documents aren't used to train models. Some of our clients are quite sensitive about that.
findings.context: Prospect requires GDPR-compliant terms and written assurance that client documents are not used to train models, because some clients are sensitive about this. — Security requirements raised by Head of Client Services; GDPR and no-model-training concern, not hosting location. Hosting or storage location was not discussed.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: And we're fully GDPR compliant, so that's all covered.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states it is fully GDPR compliant and that this covers the prospect's concern. — Vendor answer to the GDPR part of the security question, given without specifics about data location or hosting.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: We don't train on customer data. That's in the terms.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states it does not train on customer data and that this is in its terms. — Vendor answer to the model-training concern; the prospect asked for it in writing.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Can we see that in writing?
findings.context: Prospect asks for written confirmation that its data is not used for model training. — Follow-up to the vendor's verbal claim; the prospect wants documentary proof.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Course. I'll send the DPA over.
findings.context: OrbitFlow commits to send a DPA covering the training-data assurance. — Vendor commitment in response to the written request. The DPA content was not described and no hosting or residency commitment was made.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: And the written thing about model training.
findings.context: Prospect reiterates the need for the written model-training assurance as a follow-up item. — Closing action list; the prospect is still waiting on this from the vendor.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: preferably UK data residency
findings.context: Carlos Mendes stated that he would prefer UK data residency for OrbitFlow. — Security requirements list; customer-side requirement for residency, but stated as a preference.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: It was you, and it is preferably rather than mandatory. We're not regulated in that way. It's more that our procurement people prefer it.
findings.context: Lucy Hart clarified that UK data residency is preferred, not mandatory, because Greenline is not regulated in that way; the preference is driven by procurement. — Correction/clarification of Carlos's statement about residency being a requirement.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise.
findings.context: Jon Bell stated that EU data residency is available on OrbitFlow's Enterprise tier. — Vendor answer to the residency question; limited to EU and Enterprise.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: UK specifically I'd need to confirm rather than assume, and I'm not going to say yes to make the call go smoothly.
findings.context: Jon Bell declined to confirm UK-specific data residency and refused to assume it, committing instead to a definitive written answer. — Hedge on UK residency; vendor explicitly did not say yes to smooth the call.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: And from us in writing — the UK residency answer, and a note on the regional workspace and permissions design.
findings.context: Maya Chen committed to sending a written UK residency answer after the call. — Follow-up commitment from vendor on residency.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: UK residency.
findings.context: Customer requires UK data residency as one of its must-have items for the evaluation. — Samir lists his checklist for the vendor; UK residency is one of the requirements.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: UK residency?
findings.context: Customer asks directly whether OrbitFlow offers UK residency. — Follow-up question right after the vendor's answer on Enterprise SSO, SCIM and encryption.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK specifically I need to confirm in writing. I'm not going to say yes on a call.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states EU data residency is available on Enterprise, but UK residency is unconfirmed and will be confirmed in writing, not on the call. — Vendor hedge; no UK commitment made.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: EU is not UK.
findings.context: Customer insists EU hosting is not the same as UK residency and the vendor agrees. — Customer pushes back on EU-for-UK substitution; vendor concedes the distinction.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: For some of our clients that distinction matters a great deal.
findings.context: The EU-versus-UK distinction matters to some clients, particularly public sector work. — Customer explains why the residency gap is material for client and public-sector business.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: It matters for the public sector work particularly.
findings.context: Eleanor says the UK residency issue matters particularly for public sector work. — Supports Samir's point on client requirements.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Then it's a genuine open question and it may be a gate. I'll get you a definitive answer within the week.
findings.context: OrbitFlow treats UK residency as an open question that may be a deal gate, with a definitive answer promised within a week. — Vendor commitment on timing; answer not yet given in the call.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: If the answer is no, tell me it's no. Don't tell me it's on the roadmap.
findings.context: Customer wants a plain no if UK residency is unavailable, not a roadmap promise. — Customer sets a condition on how the answer is given.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: I won't dress a roadmap item as a capability.
findings.context: OrbitFlow says it will not present a roadmap item as a current capability. — Vendor response to the customer's request on roadmap framing.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Four items. UK residency, retention floor, AI-step permission granularity, and the audit payload schema.
findings.context: OrbitFlow lists UK residency as one of four open written items to be answered. — Vendor recap of outstanding questions.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Plus written answers on UK residency, the retention floor, AI-step permission granularity, the audit payload schema, and termination data handling.
findings.context: OrbitFlow commits to sending written answers on UK residency as part of next steps. — Vendor's next-steps summary; written answer is a deliverable, not yet a confirmed capability.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: FERPA. We handle data about students in US school districts. Student-level records are subject to specific protections and our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
findings.context: Prospect states student-level records are subject to FERPA protections and should never leave Inkwell's own warehouse. — Customer's stated data-location requirement tied to FERPA for US school district student data. Concerns the customer's warehouse, not OrbitFlow's hosting. No OrbitFlow hosting region or residency was discussed.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Usage counts, engagement rates, ticket volumes at the account level. Never a student record, never a student identifier.
findings.context: Prospect defines the boundary as account-level aggregates only, with no student records or student identifiers in the workflow. — Customer's stated scope for the data the workflow may use. Follows the FERPA residency requirement.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: SSO, audit logs, retention controls, and a clear boundary around student-level data. That last one is the important one.
findings.context: Prospect says a clear boundary around student-level data is the most important item on their security list. — Customer's stated priority in the security requirements, raised before the FERPA explanation.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: If the view we consume contains no student-level columns, no workflow can leak them regardless of who builds it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say the student-data constraint is easier to enforce by defining it in the Snowflake view the workflow consumes, so no workflow can leak student-level columns. — Vendor design answer to the FERPA boundary. It is a claim about the architecture the vendor proposes, not a hosting or residency commitment.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Our counsel would much rather hear "the data never leaves" than "the vendor has controls."
findings.context: Prospect says the data-never-leaves design is what counsel wants to hear, more than vendor controls. — Customer's view on how the FERPA answer should be framed to their legal team.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Regional controls — what does that mean concretely?
findings.context: Regional controls question: Ava asks what 'regional controls' means concretely, and OrbitFlow (Nina) answers that EU data residency is available on Enterprise and asks for more granularity if needed. — Vendor answer to a prospect's security-list question; vendor offers EU residency only as an Enterprise feature and leaves granular needs open.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. If you mean something more granular than that, tell me what and I'll answer specifically.
findings.context: OrbitFlow states EU data residency is available on the Enterprise tier. — Vendor claim in response to the regional controls question; tier-gated, not available on lower packages per the claim.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
findings.context: Ava states the prospect's requirement is EU data residency, based on EU customers and data residency commitments in some contracts. — Prospect defines the requirement after the vendor's answer; she frames it as 'probably' the requirement.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: It's in two contracts. Both enterprise accounts.
findings.context: Marcus Chen says the data residency commitment appears in two contracts, both enterprise accounts; Ava notes these are only the two they know about. — Prospect discloses scope of residency commitments; possible under-count acknowledged by Ava as jokingly uncertain.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: That's worth checking before an evaluation rather than after.
findings.context: Leo Grant advises checking residency commitments before the evaluation rather than after; Marcus agrees to check, and it is assigned to Marcus as an action item. — Vendor urges early verification; prospect takes ownership of checking contracts.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: I'll do the contracts.
findings.context: Ava was responsible for the residency-related Salesforce and contract checks; Marcus said he would do the contracts check. — Action item from the wrap-up: Marcus confirms he will check the two EU contracts for residency commitments.

draft.answer: Eight of ten prospects raised a residency or data-location concern, and the most common ask was EU or UK residency [C1][C2][C3][C4][C5][C6]. Acme Logistics said it has no residency requirement for this project [C7]. Greenline Energy Services prefers UK residency but does not require it [C5], and Inkwell Learning's FERPA concern is about keeping student records in its own warehouse [C8]. OrbitFlow reps consistently offered EU residency on Enterprise only, and repeatedly declined to confirm UK residency or default regions on the call, promising written answers [C9][C10].

claims.text: Harbor Legal (Samir Khan) lists UK residency as a must-have and insists EU is not UK. He says the distinction matters a great deal to some clients, and Eleanor Brooks says it matters especially for public sector work. He wants a plain no rather than a roadmap promise. Nina Patel said it may be a deal gate and promised a definitive answer within the week; UK residency is also on the written-items list.

DeltaWorks Manufacturing (Anika Bose) listed German or EU data residency as a governance requirement. Jon Bell said OrbitFlow offers EU only and has no German region. Anika said EU may be sufficient but depends on which legal entity owns the data, a question for their legal team. Martin Vogel separately said two German plants are prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors, a hosting constraint he later said was from memory.

Juniper Cloud Tools (Ava Sinclair) said EU residency is probably the requirement because of EU customers and residency commitments in some contracts. Marcus Chen said the commitment appears in two enterprise-account contracts. Leo Grant advised checking before the evaluation, and Marcus took the action to check the contracts.

Cedar & Finch (Sophie Reed) sells into the UK and EU and wants to know where customer data is processed. When told EU residency is Enterprise-only, she reacted that it is the expensive tier, and Leo Grant agreed. Leo said he would confirm the Growth plan's default processing region in writing, and later listed it as a question he dodged and owes in writing.

Greenline Energy Services: Carlos Mendes said he would preferably want UK residency, and Lucy Hart clarified it is preferred, not mandatory, because Greenline is not regulated that way and procurement prefers it. Jon Bell would not confirm UK residency and Maya Chen committed to a written UK answer.

BrightPath Health (Elliot Greene), a US operation with a UK subsidiary, asked for the default EU region. Jon Bell said it depends on where the workspace is provisioned and offered to confirm in writing; Elliot approved of that answer. Elliot's security list also included confirming how US data is handled.

Acme Logistics (Tom Alvarez) said it has no special data-residency requirement for this project. Jon Bell offered EU residency on Enterprise anyway. Tom's remark that Acme is not healthcare only implies no sector-driven rules. Jon hedged on where data sent to an LLM provider goes, saying it depends on configuration and provider.

Inkwell Learning (Darren Wu) said FERPA-covered student-level records should never leave Inkwell's warehouse and the workflow should use only account-level aggregates. Jon Bell proposed enforcing this in the Snowflake view the workflow consumes. This is a customer-warehouse boundary, not an OrbitFlow hosting region.

Ember Financial's Hannah Cole requires EU residency for European records, and Nina Patel said it is available on Enterprise. Leo Grant's list of written follow-ups does not appear to include residency.

Fable Media (Ben Foster) raised GDPR terms and written assurance of no model training, not hosting location. Alastair McCrae said OrbitFlow is fully GDPR compliant and does not train on customer data, and promised a DPA. Ben still listed the written assurance as outstanding.

Across calls, OrbitFlow reps (Jon Bell, Nina Patel, Leo Grant) repeatedly said EU residency is available on Enterprise, while declining to confirm UK residency or default regions on the call and committing to written answers.

conflicts.topic: Whether UK residency is required at Greenline
conflicts.description: Carlos Mendes stated a UK residency preference as a requirement, but Lucy Hart corrected that it is preferred and not mandatory.

conflicts.topic: Whether residency was committed in writing at Ember
conflicts.description: Nina Patel stated EU residency is available on Enterprise, but Leo Grant's follow-up list omits residency, so no written follow-up appears to exist (an inference from the omission).

not_covered: Whether any written residency answers (UK, default region) were actually delivered after the calls.
Which regions or processing locations OrbitFlow actually supports beyond EU on Enterprise.

Residency synonyms include data location, sovereignty, regional hosting and GDPR-related storage concerns.
